headline: More than 12 Egyptian developers take stands at SEREDO in Jeddah
deck: Egyptian developers are selling into a Saudi buyer base, and the construction work sits at the other end of the transaction, in Egypt.
excerpt: More than 12 Egyptian real estate development companies are participating in SEREDO 2026 in Jeddah. Cross-border property sales of this kind move buyers rather than buildings, and the construction demand they generate lands in the seller's country rather than the buyer's.
content:
More than 12 Egyptian real estate development companies are participating in the fifth edition of SEREDO in Jeddah, which opened on 6 September at the Jeddah Superdome and runs until 8 September.

A national contingent of that size at a property exhibition is a sales operation with a specific target. Egyptian developers exhibiting in Saudi Arabia are not seeking Saudi construction work; they are seeking Saudi buyers for units being built in Egypt. The transaction moves capital in one direction and leaves the construction activity where it started.

That is worth separating from the pattern this desk usually reports. Most cross-border activity in Gulf construction involves contractors and suppliers moving towards demand: a Turkish contractor bidding Saudi work, a European manufacturer opening a Riyadh service centre, an Egyptian steel producer selling into a Gulf project. Here the direction reverses. The product is finished real estate, the buyer travels nowhere, and the materials, labour and contracting all remain in Egypt.

The logic behind it is straightforward. Egypt's construction sector runs a large domestic pipeline built on new urban communities, housing and transport, and its materials industry has repeatedly carried installed capacity ahead of what the home market absorbs. Selling completed and off-plan units to buyers outside the country converts that capacity into foreign currency without the developer having to win work abroad.

For the Saudi side, the presence is a feature of an exhibition that positions itself as a meeting point for the sector rather than a purely domestic showcase. Buyers walking the floor at SEREDO can compare a Jeddah scheme with a Cairo one, which is a different proposition from comparing two Jeddah schemes, and the organisers have evidently decided that comparison is part of what the event offers.

There is a second-order effect that matters to suppliers. A Saudi buyer who places capital in an Egyptian unit has not placed it in a Saudi one, and the residential segment is where the largest number of independent Saudi developers compete for exactly that capital. Whether the flow is material at the scale of the market is not something an exhibition floor can answer, but the competition is now visible in one hall.

The Egyptian participation sits alongside the Saudi government and financing presence at the show, where the General Authority for Real Estate is a legislative partner, the Real Estate Development Fund covers the financing sector and the National Housing Company is a main sponsor.

The practical question for a Saudi supplier is whether any of this changes what gets ordered. In the short term it does not: a unit sold in Cairo is procured in Cairo, from Egyptian cement, Egyptian reinforcement and an Egyptian contractor. The longer-term reading is about where a fragmented residential buyer base places its money when it is given a wider menu, and that is a question the next few editions of this exhibition will answer more usefully than this one.
author: Jakson Gudawela
